Neonatal Iberian lynx emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably modest size, with newborn cubs weighing approximately 350 grams [Wwb = approximately 350 grams]. This initial mass, typical of altricial carnivores, belies the rapid growth trajectory that follows during the suckling stage, when the cubs are entirely dependent on their mother's milk. The nursing offspring remain in the natal den for several months, undergoing a critical period of mass gain and developmental maturation. Under the typical body temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C] that characterises the active metabolic phase of adult lynx, the gestation period that precedes parturition lasts 68 days [tg = 68 days]. This relatively short intrauterine development, given the eventual adult size of the species, reflects the energetic constraints faced by the gravid female, who must sustain herself on a diet of European rabbit while supporting foetal organogenesis. The comparability of gestation length to other medium-sized felids underscores the phylogenetic conservatism of reproductive timing within the Felidae, even in this critically endangered apex predator.

Sexual maturation in the Iberian lynx is a protracted process relative to its body size, with female cubs attaining puberty at approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth] when maintained at a core temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. This extended period of juvenile development is unusual among field species of comparable mass and likely reflects the high ecological demands imposed by a specialised, low-density prey base. During the post-weaning stage, sub-adult females must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves before their first oestrous cycle can be successfully initiated. The timing of reproductive activation is tightly linked to body condition, with leaner yearlings often delaying their first ovulation by an additional season. This reproductive strategy fits the broader life-history pattern of the species, which prioritises somatic growth and resource acquisition over precocious breeding. The age at first reproduction therefore exhibits notable interannual variation, contingent upon local rabbit abundance and territory quality.

Female Iberian lynx ultimately attain a maximum recorded adult body mass of 9600 grams [Wwi = 9600 grams], while males are significantly larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 12000 grams [Wwi = 12000 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males exceeding females by roughly 25 percent, is common among solitary, territorial felids where intramale competition for breeding territories is intense. The larger body frame of males confers advantages in defending high-quality home ranges that overlap with multiple females, thereby maximising their access to mating opportunities. The evolution of such a marked mass disparity reflects selective pressures acting on male contest ability, balanced against the energetic costs of maintaining a larger body in a resource-scarce Mediterranean scrubland environment. Body mass in both sexes shows seasonal fluctuation, reaching a nadir during the late summer rabbit scarcity and peaking in early winter prior to the main mating season in January and February.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Iberian lynx, based on comparative data from its congener the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx), is estimated at approximately 23.7 years [am = approximately 23.7 years] under the typical body temperature regime of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. This substantial longevity is characteristic of slow-living carnivores that invest heavily in each offspring, producing small litters with a high degree of maternal care. Field records from the Doñana and Sierra Morena populations indicate that individuals may survive well into their second decade, though senescence becomes evident after about 15 years through reduced hunting efficiency and declining reproductive output. The long reproductive window afforded by this lifespan allows females to compensate for low annual fecundity by breeding repeatedly across many seasons. In captivity, where veterinary care and consistent food supply eliminate external mortality sources, individual longevity may even exceed the wild estimate, approaching three decades under optimal management. This life-history strategy contrasts sharply with smaller, fast-lived mammalian predators.

Weaning in the Iberian lynx occurs approximately 259 days after birth [tx = approximately 259 days after birth], based on a typical range of 7 to 10 months of lactation-supported dependency observed in field studies at a temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. At this stage, the milk-dependent young transition to a diet of solid prey, initially consuming rabbit carcasses provisioned by the mother before learning to hunt independently. The extended nursing phase is energetically costly for the lactating female, who must increase her food intake substantially to sustain milk production for a litter of typically two pups [N_R_i = a litter of typically two pups]. The maximum reproductive rate, calculated as approximately 2 to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 litters per year], results in a modest annual output that is compensated by high offspring survival under favourable conditions. This conservative reproductive output, measured against the body temperature baseline of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], aligns with the species' status as a K-selected predator specialised on a fluctuating prey resource.
